newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bayer advances on news of R&D spending hike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bayer advances on news of R&D spending hike.

text.p: Shares in German chemicals giant Bayer AG advanced over three percent on Thursday after the group said it planned to spend a record 3.7 billion marks ($2.2 billion) on research and development in 1997.
The market welcomed the news and Bayer stock was up 2.25 marks at 71.25 marks in late bourse trade and was one of the most heavily traded stocks in floor trade in Frankfurt.
Bayer went on to say it had around a dozen drugs in development with a sales potential of over 10 billion marks.

"We have a well-stocked product pipeline in our health care segment -- especially the pharmaceuticals business group -- and in the crop protection and animal health care business groups," Bayer's chief executive Manfred Schneider told a company meeting late on Wednesday.

Christine Dienhart, chemicals analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank in Munich, said: "The fact that Bayer gets more bang for its buck on its R&D spending, especially on the pharamceutical side, makes it attractive to the markets."

"The main reason we see for Bayer's current success is that it looks good technically. We have seen people switching into Bayer out of Hoechst AG. Bayer will show growth this year and gives good dividend yields," said Dienhart.
Products under development for plant protection were expected to add a minimum 500 million marks in new sales.

He said that 2.5 billion marks of the funds allocated for R&D were earmarked for healthcare and agriculture, while additional funds would be spent on new product development as well as on marketing efforts.
Bayer said it was not considering whether cells from cloned animals should be used for testing of human medicines.
Genetic experiments have been a controversial issue since British scientists recently announced they had cloned a sheep by using the cell of an adult sheep.
Peter Stadtler, the director of Bayer's biotechnology division, said that Bayer had no interest in developing ways to change gene technology in humans.

The group would continue to look abroad, especially to the tiger economies of the Pacific Rim. Schneider said Bayer will step up its investment plans in Asia earlier than expected to more than two billion marks during the next five years.
Some of the funds have been earmarked for a polycarbonate plant in Thailand and a polyeurethane plant in Taiwan. Funds will also be spent to increase research in the region.
57 percent of Bayer's research budget was still spent in Germany but that amount was expected to drop in the coming years, Schneider said.
He said, however, that Bayer was not reducing its work in Germany, where it employs 60 percent of the 14,000 people at the company involved in research.
Schneider also said Bayer would introduce two new medicines in the next two years, including one against septic shock.
On the subject of the group's structure, Schneider also said he expected the German chemicals group to remain independent going into the next century.

"It is unimaginable that a business with a market value of about 50 billion marks would not remain independent," Schneider said, adding that Bayer must improve its return on sales from the current level of about 10 percent.
"We must do better and we will do better," he said.

He said Bayer was in a good position with its life sciences area, which includes healthcare and agriculture, as well as in the polymer division. But he said Bayer was having problems in its standard chemicals business that mainly come from Germany.
In addition, Schneider said it would be a success if the number of workers at Bayer's five plants in Germany were to remain stable at the current level of about 48,000 workers.
($ = 1.687 German Marks)
